title: 'You Just Saved the Video Dish': Astronauts Complete Critical Spacewalk Repair
summary:
On Tuesday, August 25, two astronauts floated outside the International Space Station (ISS) to fix a crucial piece of equipment: a Space-to-Ground Antenna (SGANT) that had stopped working last November. Without it, the station couldn't reliably track NASA's data relay satellites, threatening voice and video communication with Earth.

Anil Menon of NASA and Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency (ESA) spent exactly 6.5 hours on the spacewalk, from 8:27 a.m. to 2:57 p.m. EDT. Menon, positioned at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm, retrieved a spare antenna from an external storage location. Adenot traversed by handrails to join him, and together they mounted the new dish on the Z-1 truss, connecting it to power and data systems. Then they moved the faulty antenna to a more permanent storage spot on the station's backbone truss.

This was the 283rd spacewalk in support of ISS assembly and maintenance. It was Menon's third EVA, bringing his total spacewalking time to 19 hours and 20 minutes. For Adenot, it was her second spacewalk, raising her total to 12 hours and 53 minutes—and she holds the distinction of being the first woman and fifth French citizen to perform a spacewalk.

The repair restores redundancy to the communication system, meaning the station now has two working antennas again. Mission Control celebrated with a playful parody of The Buggles' 1979 hit "Video Killed the Radio Star": "On behalf of CAPCOM and I, we're going to count down like a bolt: '3, 2, 1... You just saved the video dish, you just saved the video dish.'" Menon laughed, replying, "Oh my god, it is hard to top that. I want to thank the entire team on executing this complex, time-critical operation successfully."

This spacewalk was the sixth from the ISS this year and the 98th using U.S. spacesuits. It's a reminder of the intricate, high-stakes work astronauts do to keep the station—and our connection to space—running smoothly.
why_it_matters: Communication is the lifeline between astronauts and Earth; losing it would threaten both safety and the science done on the station. This repair also shows how international teams solve high-stakes problems in space, a lesson for future missions.

background_read: The International Space Station (ISS)—a football-field-sized laboratory that orbits Earth about every 90 minutes—has been continuously home to astronauts since 2000.
It uses antennas like the Space-to-Ground Antenna (SGANT) to send voice, video, and data through a network of relay satellites so Mission Control can stay in contact.

NASA (the United States' space agency) and the European Space Agency (ESA, a partnership of European countries) are leading partners in the station, and astronauts from both agencies regularly work outside during spacewalks.
Spacewalks are officially called EVAs, and hundreds have been performed to build and maintain the ISS.
The Canadarm2, a large robotic arm built by Canada, helps astronauts by carrying them or equipment to work sites, as it did in this repair.

perspectives.description: For NASA and ESA, the successful repair restores full communication redundancy, so mission controllers and crews regain a reliable backup. It also demonstrates that astronauts can execute complex, time-sensitive procedures under unforgiving conditions.

The antenna failure itself is a reminder of how fragile critical space infrastructure can be; if the repair had failed, voice and video links with Earth could have been compromised. It also highlights the toll of maintaining aging systems in orbit, where a single equipment failure can require a risky spacewalk.

Spacewalks like this are routine but high-stakes operations, logged in a long history of ISS maintenance that now numbers 283 EVAs. The careful choreography—using a robotic arm, moving antennas, checking connections—follows years of preparation and shared international procedures.

As space agencies plan longer missions beyond Earth orbit, reliable communication networks and repair strategies will only become more essential. Lessons from this repair could shape how future stations and spacecraft design antennas that are easier to fix or replace.
